You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

The flexibility and intelligent responsiveness of hydrogel robots offer great potential for exploration in narrow and complex environments. However, the integration of sensors with hydrogel robotic bodies remains challenging. Inspired by marine organisms, this paper presents an anemone-like light-driven hydrogel robot (ALHR) for directional infrared radiation detection. We fabricated via ultrasonic-assisted stacking a black phosphorus/tungsten disulfide (BP/WS2) moiré superlattice, showing high dual-mode photothermal-photovoltaic conversion performance. Based on this, a composite poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) hydrogel was used to build the base plate and tentacle structures of the ALHR. Specific illumination was found to trigger the photothermal effect of the BP/WS2 moiré superlattice, allowing for directional movement. When the tentacles retract and contact the bottom electrode, photocurrent signals are conducted for infrared detection. The ALHR can work in specialized spatial environments, providing a promising method for early overheating fault identification in equipment. This study proposes a universal design framework for multifunctional hydrogel robots by integrating responsive units with driving units to leverage the synergistic effects of multiple materials.

---

## Introduction

Flexible hydrogel robots with biomimetic structures show great application potential in complex scenarios that humans can’t access, like deep-sea exploration, confined spaces, and high-radiation environments. This is due to their excellent biocompatibility, deformability, and environmental adaptability1–4. By integrating functional units such as sensors and actuators into hydrogel matrices to imitate the morphology and behavior of natural organisms, researchers can effectively combine the unique physicochemical properties of hydrogels with the excellent capabilities of biological systems5–8. This method gives robots intelligent features like autonomous mobility and real-time perception, creating opportunities for the development of flexible bionic robots9–11. However, two main bottlenecks still exist in this field. Firstly, the high water content and softness of hydrogels often reduce the performance and stability of integrated sensors, making traditional microelectronic fabrication techniques inappropriate. Secondly, current research mainly focuses on achieving single functions (such as actuation or drug delivery) and has difficulty in balancing robotic mobility and sensing capabilities. Achieving the integration of actuation-sensing remains a challenging task12,13. Therefore, how to enhance the response speed, structural stability, and sensing compatibility of hydrogel robots simultaneously through innovative material and structural design has become a crucial scientific problem that needs urgent solutions in this field.

To tackle these challenges, exploring materials that combine both actuation and sensing functions is a key breakthrough. Among different actuation strategies, light-driven actuation is regarded as an ideal option for building smart hydrogel robots. This is because it is non-contact, highly precise, has a rapid response, and excellent biocompatibility14–20. Among them, poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM), due to its excellent thermosensitive properties, has become a typical material system for preparing photodriven hydrogels when combined with photothermal converters21–23. Traditional methods rely on complex integrated designs to couple sensing and driving functions, but this makes the system even more unstable11,24. Therefore, developing an innovative structural composite material with both photothermal actuation and optoelectronic sensing capabilities is the fundamental solution to the sensor-hydrogel compatibility problem.

According to the latest research findings, the emerging moiré superlattice materials have demonstrated excellent performance that can meet various requirements. This periodic structure, formed by stacking two two-dimensional (2D) materials with different lattice constants or orientations25,26, provides a unique moiré potential field. This field can effectively adjust interlayer exciton dynamics, phonon vibration modes, and band structures, offering a platform for synergistically optimizing photothermal and photovoltaic performance27–36. Despite the great potential of moiré superlattices, current research mainly focuses on systems such as graphene. There is still limited systematic exploration of heterojunctions and their dual-function characteristics involving BP, a material with an inherently high photothermal coefficient, and other 2D materials.

This work introduces a universal framework to realize multifunctional integrated hydrogel robots. At the materials level, we designed and synthesized black phosphorus/tungsten disulfide (BP/WS2) moiré superlattices using an ultrasonic-assisted stacking method. The moiré potential field in this material enhances phonon-photon coupling to improve photothermal conversion efficiency while simultaneously promoting the separation and transport of photogenerated carriers, resulting in dual photothermal-photovoltaic response characteristics. At the design level, inspired by sea anemone feeding behavior, we integrated the BP/WS2 moiré superlattice with a PNIPAM flexible matrix to construct an anemone-like light-driven hydrogel robot (ALHR). The base plate generates photothermal effects under illumination to drive directional motion, while the tentacles sense infrared radiation and produce photocurrent signals, effectively integrating coordinated motion and sensing. Furthermore, the photothermal driving capability of ALHR enables it to adapt well to various complex environments and confined spaces. Its photoelectric conversion ability allows for the detection of overheated areas of the equipment, demonstrating its potential as an overheating monitoring robot. Finally, we propose a universal strategy centered on function-oriented moiré superlattice-hydrogels, where modular integration and synergistic coupling of responsive units with flexible substrates enable on-demand design of intelligent soft robots with diverse sensing and actuation capabilities. This research not only provides materials and methods for high-performance integrated actuator-sensor robots but also establishes a universal technical pathway and design paradigm for future multifunctional soft robots based on advanced 2D materials.

---

## Results

Structural design and synthesis
Inspired by the structural and functional elegance of sea anemones37, we have developed an ALHR, as depicted in Fig. 1a. The ALHR features a large, soft base plate that mimics the anemone’s ability to anchor itself, serving as a brake during movement. The base plate is primarily composed of a BP/WS2-PNIPAM composite hydrogel, synthesized via a one-pot cross-linking method using N-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAM) as the polymer monomer and a homogeneously dispersed BP/WS2 moiré superlattice as the photothermal agent. The tentacle-like structures are made of standard PNIPAM hydrogel, coated with a BP/WS2 film on the surface, enabling light sensing and morphologic changes akin to those of anemone tentacles. The BP/WS2 moiré superlattice is pivotal to the ALHR’s functionality, exhibiting photothermal and photovoltaic properties due to its unique structure38. The BP/WS2 moiré superlattice, prepared through an ultrasound-assisted stacking method, leverages the slight lattice mismatch between BP and WS2. This mismatch creates long-periodic moiré patterns, enhancing near-infrared light absorption and enabling superior photovoltaic and photothermal conversion capabilities. As illustrated in Fig. 1a (right inset), the BP/WS2-PNIPAM composite hydrogel undergoes thermal-induced contraction under the driving light source (like 660 nm light), leading to bending and deformation. Upon light cessation, the hydrogel reabsorbs water and returns to its original state, driving the robot’s movement through friction. The direction of movement is precisely controllable. The tentacle’s BP/WS2 functional layer detects infrared radiation from overheated areas, triggering both photothermal and photoelectric effects. The photothermal effect causes localized warming and contraction, while the photoelectric effect converts light energy into exciton energy, generating a photocurrent (Fig. 1a, left inset). Here, we chose 660 nm light as the driving light source since this wavelength is different from the required detection signal band. Additionally, 660 nm light irradiation causes a weak photothermal response in the BP/WS2 moiré superlattice, leading to a slight temperature rise. This mildly drives the phase transition of the hydrogel in the substrate layer and avoids excessive water loss that might damage its internally stable cross-linked structure. Its weak response property also reduces the interference to the monitoring system caused by the tentacle contraction induced by the driving light source. This dual-response mechanism ensures accurate, real-time overheating detection. As shown in Fig. 1b, the ALHR operates through two primary functional modules: movement driven by the base plate and detection facilitated by the tentacles. When illuminated by a light source (such as 660 nm light), the base plate’s BP/WS2 photothermal agent converts light into heat, causing water loss and deformation in the hydrogel. This reversible bending-straightening cycle, regulated by light, propels the ALHR in a specific direction. Upon approaching an overheating source, the tentacle’s BP/WS2 layer detects near-infrared radiation (such as 808 nm wavelength), inducing a photothermal response that contracts the PNIPAM hydrogel. This contraction brings the functional layer into contact with a bottom electrode, conducting a photocurrent that signals the overheating location. When the ALHR moves away, the photothermal effect diminishes, the tentacle returns to its original form, and the electrical signal ceases. This reversible contact-disengagement cycle enables precise overheating detection, leveraging the synergistic effects of photothermal and photoelectric responses.

Characterization of moiré superlattices
The synthesis and characterization of BP/WS2 moiré superlattices constitute the cornerstone of the ALHR’s overheating detection functionality. Bulk BP powder was first prepared via high-energy ball milling using red phosphorus as the precursor. Few-layer BP nanosheets were subsequently obtained through ultrasound-assisted liquid-phase exfoliation. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Fig. 2a) provided conclusive evidence that the van der Waals forces existing between the BP layers were disrupted. This disruption was attributed to the substantial energy released upon the rupture of ultrasonic cavitation bubbles39. As a result, the successful synthesis of BP was achieved. Concurrently, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images (Supplementary Fig. 1) revealed that the as-prepared BP nanosheets possessed clearly defined edges and distinctive lamellar structures. The size distributions of these nanosheets fell within the range of 10-20 μm, endowing them with excellent specific surface area characteristics. WS2 nanosheets were synthesized using chemical vapor deposition (CVD), wherein sulfur vapor reacted with WO3 vapor deposited on silicon wafers in a dual-temperature zone tube furnace. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 2, the WS2 nanosheets exhibit the characteristic lamellar structure of 2D materials, with sizes ranging from 100 to 200 nm, smaller than those of the BP nanosheets. The XRD patterns of WS2 display characteristic peaks corresponding to the (002), (004), (104), and (110) crystallographic planes, which align well with the standard 2H-phase WS2 reference, confirming its high crystallinity and specific crystalline structure. To construct the BP/WS2 moiré superlattice, an inkjet printing technique was employed to uniformly deposit an ultra-low concentration of BP nanosheet dispersion onto the surface of WS2, followed by thorough drying to ensure intimate contact. The XRD patterns of the resulting composite reveal characteristic peaks of WS2 at 2θ = 16.5°, 37.7°, and 68.6°, alongside peaks at 38° and 57.8° attributed to BP. Additionally, the broad, bun-like peaks of BP between 10° and 30° are preserved in the composite. Notably, the dominance of WS2 peaks in the composite is primarily due to the relatively low loading ratio of BP, while the weakened intensity of the (020) peak of BP may result from changes in the number of layers along the stacking direction and slight lattice distortions induced by the formation of the moiré superlattice. Raman spectral analysis (Fig. 2b) provides further insights into the vibrational modes of the BP/WS2 composite. The in-plane vibrational modes of BP are observed at 360 cm-1 and 470 cm-1, while the out-of-plane vibrational modes exhibit significant shifts compared to intrinsic BP (Supplementary Fig. 3). These shifts are primarily attributed to the modification of atomic vibrational environments induced by interlayer coupling and the moiré potential field, which arise from the formation of the moiré superlattice. This results in changes in phonon frequencies, manifesting as a redshift of the Raman characteristic peaks. Similarly, the in-plane vibrational mode of WS2 is observed at 350 cm-1, with its out-of-plane vibrational mode also slightly shifted relative to intrinsic WS2 (Supplementary Fig. 4). This indicates that the phonon vibrational modes of WS2 are similarly modulated by the moiré potential, leading to a weakening of the vibrational frequencies. At the microscopic level, the BP/WS2 moiré superlattice is characterized by large BP sheets encapsulating smaller WS2 sheets (Fig. 2c). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images clearly reveal the layered morphology and distribution states of the 2D materials. As shown in Fig. 2d, the lattice spacings of BP (0.46 nm) and WS2 (0.25 nm) are simultaneously observable along the b-axis direction. Due to the significant difference in lattice constants between the two materials, their atomic arrangements do not completely overlap when stacked together. Instead, as illustrated in Fig. 2e, periodic dislocation and overlap regions form, where the atomic interactions in the dislocation regions differ from those in the overlap regions. This results in a larger-scale periodic modulation across the entire stacked structure, known as the moiré pattern. Furthermore, the orthorhombic crystal structure of BP and the hexagonal crystal structure of WS2 possess different symmetries. When these materials are stacked to form a moiré superlattice, their distinct symmetries complement and influence each other, generating a symmetry feature. The TEM and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) images in Fig. 2f further corroborate the formation of a periodic pattern with a larger scale, confirming the presence of a moiré superlattice between BP and WS2 due to the interference of their atomic layers. The changes in the interfacial electronic states also reflect the modulation of the moiré superlattice. As shown in Fig. 2g, compared to the intrinsic materials, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) shows that the BP/WS2 moiré superlattice displays characteristic peaks at 32.7 eV and 34.8 eV, corresponding to the W 4f7/2 and W 4f5/2 orbitals, respectively, with an overall redshift. Additionally, the excitation of 5p3/2 orbital electrons is observed. This phenomenon suggests that the moiré potential modulates the electron cloud density of W atoms. The formation of flat bands and increased electron localization induces a quantum confinement effect, causing electrons to preferentially occupy confined orbitals. Consequently, the excess energy of the X-ray electrons used in the test excites the 5p3/2 orbital electrons. A similar effect is observed for the S atoms (Fig. 2h), while the increased binding energy of the P 2p orbital electrons (Fig. 2i) confirms their role as electron donors in the composite. The interlayer coupling alters the overall electron cloud distribution, enhancing electron localization near the W atoms. According to the binding energy calculation formula, the composite material (Fig. 2j) exhibit significantly higher electron binding energy compared to intrinsic BP (Supplementary Fig. 5) and WS2 (Supplementary Fig. 6), indicating stronger electron binding. This modulation profoundly influences the light absorption properties of the system. For WS2, the Fermi level shift shows that the moiré potential effectively adjusts the potential energy distribution of W atoms near the interface, causing the localization of their electron clouds. When electrons are localized around W atoms, their shielding effect on the inner-shell electrons of W 4f is strengthened. According to Coulomb’s law, this strengthened shielding weakens the nucleus’s effective attraction to the 4f electrons, thus reducing their binding energy. In composite materials, BP serves as an electron donor. It transfers electrons to WS2, which in turn reduces the surface electron density of WS2. This enhances the ability of atomic nuclei to confine electrons, leading to an increase in the work function compared to the intrinsic material. As illustrated in Fig. 2k, the composite material integrates the absorption peaks of both BP and WS2, with a notably enhanced absorption in the infrared band. This confirms the effective modulation of the material’s optical properties. Furthermore, based on the light absorption characteristics (Fig. 2l), the band gap of the composite is calculated to be approximately 1.93 eV, consistent with the expected results.

Optical properties and response mechanisms
BP/WS2 moiré superlattices exhibit different physical phenomena that are markedly distinct from those of their intrinsic counterparts, owing to their unique interlayer coupling and energy band modulation properties. Through systematic experiments, we demonstrate that the BP/WS2 moiré superlattice achieves highly efficient light-to-heat energy conversion under optical excitation. As illustrated in Fig. 3a, the system temperature exhibits a significant increase with irradiation time. Notably, this photothermal conversion behavior is observed across multiple wavelength bands (Fig. 3b), with the 808 nm band being particularly prominent: the system temperature rapidly rises from an initial 22 °C to 51.9 °C within 600 s of irradiation, achieving a temperature increase of 29.9 °C. This result aligns closely with the material’s light absorption spectrum characteristics shown in Fig. 2k. Furthermore, the BP/WS2 moiré superlattice demonstrates excellent reproducibility in photothermal conversion (Fig. 3c). In periodic light-switching experiments, the system responds rapidly to optical stimuli and recovers stably to the initial temperature after irradiation ceases, highlighting the remarkable stability of its photothermal effect. Quantitative analysis of the photothermal conversion efficiency (PCE) based on established formulas40 reveals that the BP/WS2 moiré superlattice outperforms single-component WS2 in the UV and NIR bands, particularly at 808 nm, where its PCE reaches an impressive 72.1% (Fig. 3d). Further investigations reveal that the BP/WS2 moiré superlattice efficiently converts photon energy: a portion is dissipated as heat through phonon vibrations, while the remainder is transported by photogenerated carriers to generate photocurrent. Under a bias range of −2 to 2 V, the current under illumination significantly exceeds that in the dark state (Fig. 3e), confirming the material’s photo-responsive properties. Even more remarkable are the zero-bias experimental results (Fig. 3f): the photocurrent response exhibits strong wavelength dependence, with particularly high photoelectric conversion efficiencies at 405, 610, 808, and 940 nm, consistent with the light absorption spectrum. Notably, the 808 nm band generates a maximum photocurrent of 514.2 nA at zero bias, with photocurrent intensity positively correlated with light intensity (Fig. 3g). We also performed continuous spectral photoresponse testing on the BP/WS2 thin film (Supplementary Fig. 7). The results demonstrate that the device exhibit significant photoresponse capabilities across multiple bands in the ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared regions, with particularly performance in the near-infrared band. At the same low power density, multiple representative spectral bands (405, 532, 650, 808 and 940 nm) were selected for independent irradiation experiments. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 8, the results demonstrate that even at such low light intensities, the device maintains observable and relatively stable photoresponse signals in the near-infrared band. In contrast, response signals in the other tested bands are significantly weaker, falling below the effective detection threshold. To fully characterize the photovoltaic properties, we calculated the responsivity (R) and specific detectivity (D*)41, defined as:

R = (Ip - Id) / (PS) (1)

D* = RS0.5 / (2eId)0.5 (2)

Where Ip and Id denote the currents under illumination and in the dark, respectively, P is the optical power density, and S is the effective light-receiving area. The BP/WS2 moiré superlattice exhibits optoelectronic performance, as shown in Fig. 3h, with a maximum responsivity of 4.14 A/W and a specific detectivity as high as 12 × 1011 Jones. Additionally, the material demonstrates rapid response times, with rise and fall times of 70 ms and 48 ms, respectively (Fig. 3i), indicating its ability to swiftly adapt to optical signal changes. As elucidated by experimental data (Supplementary Figs. 9–14) and a direct comparison (Fig. 3j), the BP/WS2 moiré superlattice surpasses the performance of pristine BP and WS2 in both photothermal conversion and photovoltaic applications, particularly under 808 nm illumination. Compared to other similar materials, it demonstrates an overall leading edge across multiple performance parameters (Fig. 3k, Supplementary Table 1), underscoring its potential for advanced optoelectronic and energy conversion applications.

The photothermal and photoelectric response mechanisms of BP/WS2 were investigated using first-principles calculations. The results show that the work function of the composite material is approximately 4.791 eV, lying between those of BP and WS2, suggesting intermediate electron confinement capability (Supplementary Figs. 15–19). When illuminated, the composite efficiently absorbs photon energy and generates carriers on its surface. Some of this energy is released through non-equilibrium carrier recombination, while another portion is captured by defect energy levels within the bandgap and subsequently re-emitted to the conduction band. During this relaxation process, phonon scattering occurs, converting photon energy into thermal energy. In the BP/WS2 moiré superlattice, periodic moiré potential wells confine interlayer excitons, greatly extending their lifetime. As these excitons relax, they preferentially transfer energy to the lattice through nonradiative recombination, emitting phonons. This mechanism synergistically combines BP’s inherent photothermal properties with the confinement effect of the moiré potential, markedly enhancing photothermal conversion efficiency. Band structure analysis of the three components (Supplementary Fig. 20-26) indicates that the moiré superlattice significantly modulates the composite’s band structure, generating numerous flat bands with corresponding peaks in the density of states. Within these bands, electron density is relatively high, forming localized states. Driven by interlayer coupling from the moiré potential field, these localized states are periodically distributed across the system, regulating charge distribution in the barrier region. This confinement enhances electron aggregation and restricts carrier diffusion, requiring greater energy for transitions across energy barriers. The resulting confined electron-hole pairs are known as moiré excitons, which remain stable even at room temperature. For the BP/WS2 moiré superlattice, the enhanced localized states raise the energy required for non-equilibrium carriers to cross these barriers. Interestingly, the photothermal effect partially facilitates this process. The competition and synergy between these effects improve carrier separation and transport. Additionally, the modulation of the band structure by the moiré superlattice leads to more selective light absorption in the system.

Functionality of ALHR devices and expansion
Leveraging the photothermal and photoelectric response properties of BP/WS2 moiré superlattice materials, we designed an ALHR by integrating this material into a hydrogel system. The BP/WS2 moiré superlattice serves dual roles as both a photothermal driving agent and a thermal sensing material. As illustrated in Fig. 4a, the ALHR mimics the structure of an anemone, comprising two main components: a mobile basal disk and responsive tentacles. The tentacle-like structures were fabricated using a one-step method in a specific mold. PNIPAM hydrogels were prepared using NIPAM as the polymer monomer and N,N’-Methylenebisacrylamide (BIS) as the cross-linking agent. The BP/WS2 film was subsequently coated onto the top of these hydrogels. The temperature-sensitive PNIPAM hydrogels exhibit shrinking and deformation under the photothermal effect of BP/WS2, with the tentacle shape guiding the downward contraction. The basal disk of the ALHR was similarly prepared using a specific mold. The material composition is analogous to that of the tentacles, with the addition of BP/WS2 moiré superlattice material uniformly dispersed within the hydrogel network. This ensures that when any part of the basal disk is exposed to specific light, the BP/WS2 material rapidly heats the exposed area due to its superior photothermal conversion capability. The resulting temperature increase causes localized shrinkage and buckling of the hydrogel due to water loss. Upon cessation enabling the ALHR to perform walking movements akin to those of an anemone. The compatibility of materials between the tentacles and basal disk facilitates straightforward assembly, culminating in the final preparation of the robot as depicted in Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 27.

To validate the ALHR’s capability for motion and overheating detection, we conducted a series of tests. First, we examined the response of the basal disk material to light. As shown in Fig. 4c, under 660 nm light, the basal disk exhibited a consistent and uniform temperature increase of approximately 14.4 °C. This behavior demonstrated reversibility and stability in periodic switching tests (Fig. 4d) and was directly correlated with light intensity (Fig. 4e). Stronger light intensities generated more heat, enabling the system temperature to exceed the lower critical solution temperature of the PNIPAM hydrogel, initiating the phase transition.

We irradiated one side of the basal disk with 660-nm red light, which induced shrinkage deformation on the illuminated side of the basal disk. Under the influence of high-temperature conditions, this side gradually warped without experiencing complete water loss. This warping led to the contraction of the base plate, causing its tail end to move forward. After a certain period, when the light source was removed, the temperature decreased, and the basal disk relaxed. Relying on friction, the base plate accomplished light-driven peristaltic motion. Due to the differences in their own morphological structures and irradiation methods, the basal disk and tentacles exhibit completely distinct deformation behaviors, as shown in the Supplementary Fig. 28. To assess performance degradation under different conditions, we first placed tentacle samples in an unencapsulated, open environment at room temperature. As shown in Fig. 4g, the results showed that after 7 days, their response speed remained above 85% of the initial value. We found that the total weight loss rate was about 12% over 7 days, which closely matched the performance degradation rate. This confirms that water evaporation is the main factor affecting long-term performance. Figure 4h shows the drive performance stability of the base plate under continuous on-off light cycles (660 nm laser, 19 mW/cm2, 120 seconds per cycle). The base plate changes as illustrated in the diagram. The results indicate that after 200 cycles (about 6.7 hours in total), the decay rate of the base plate’s bending angle was below 5%, and the response speed remained basically unchanged. This demonstrates that our robot has excellent cyclic operational stability and fatigue resistance. We mainly attribute this remarkable stability to the dense three-dimensional network structure of the PNIPAM hydrogel, which can effectively hold a large number of water molecules. Moreover, our BP/WS2 moiré superlattice has high photothermal conversion efficiency, lowering the energy threshold for actuation. This enables a rapid response at lower overall temperatures, thus minimizing excessive heating of the hydrogel and the associated intense thermal evaporation effects.

Under illumination at a wavelength of 660 nm, the base plate undergoes a periodic bending-straightening cycle (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Movies 1 and 3). Specifically, rapid photothermal heating induces upward bending at the disk center and forward retraction of its rear end; upon light removal, cooling restores the structure to its original configuration. Driven by friction, the front edge advances forward, yielding the morphology observed in the physical image on the left. This process exhibits excellent repeatability, enabling the light-driven disk to achieve an average crawling speed of approximately 2 mm/s under modulated illumination. Our ALHR demonstrates distinct advantages over previously reported designs, as shown in Supplementary Table 242–46. Experimental testing has confirmed that our ALHR showcases remarkable motion performance. It can adapt to a wide range of media and different pipeline conditions, enabling efficient optical actuation and flexible locomotion (refer to Supplementary Table 3). In contrast, under 808 nm near-infrared light irradiation (which mimics thermal radiation), the tentacle mainly undergoes a contraction-expansion cycle: light triggers downward contraction, which is followed by slow recovery after illumination ceases, as shown in the inset. Owing to its geometric constraint, this motion occurs primarily along the vertical axis as illustrated (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Movie 2). The described behaviors were experimentally verified. During actuation, the light intensity of the driving source significantly influences the locomotion speed of the disk (Fig. 5c), showing a positive correlation with the former. Furthermore, the speed also increases with the on-off switching frequency of the light (Fig. 5d). Experimental measurements indicate that the maximum locomotion speed is attained at a frequency of 0.6 Hz. Beyond deformation, the tentacle’s detection functionality was also verified. We fixed two contact electrodes at a specific height on the tentacle’s base. As shown in the illustration, only when the tentacle contracted under the photothermal drive of BP/WS2 did the BP/WS2 at the top contact the electrodes, enabling rapid conduction of photogenerated carriers to transmit electrical signals externally (Fig. 5e, Supplementary Movie 4 and Fig. 29). No current was detected in the loop without contact, while the current magnitude varied with light intensity during contact. We also evaluated the spatial resolution of the temperature detection system. After securing a black body heat source, the entire ALHR was mounted on a precision-movable platform and translated along a straight line toward and away from the heat source. During this motion, the ALHR transitioned from the ‘non-overheated’ to the ‘overheated’ state at position x1, where the tentacle contacted the bottom electrode, and reverted to the ‘non-overheated’ state at position x2 when the tentacle detached from the bottom electrode. This procedure was repeated 50 times. The spatial resolution was defined as:

Δx = x2 - x1 (3)

Among them, x1 and x2 represent the average values of multiple sets of test data for x1 and x2, respectively. The results show that the spatial resolution of ALHR is 2.037 m. In scenarios where overheating detection is needed in complex pipelines and similar environments, our ALHR can move flexibly under the action of light. When it senses near-infrared radiation from an overheating point, it rapidly generates an electrical signal, thus reporting the overheating risk to the external environment. To verify its performance, we simulated the cooling oil lines inside a transformer using a 50-mm-diameter smooth-surfaced plastic water supply pipe with an elbow. As shown in Fig. 5g, the whole experiment was carried out in a dark, room-temperature, atmospheric environment. Thermocouple probes with controlled temperatures were placed every 10 centimeters to simulate overheating sources, and the temperature of each thermocouple was labeled on the curve. Experimental results have shown that the ALHR can respond promptly to temperatures ranging from 380 to 453 K during its movement. Thanks to its excellent flexibility and deformability, the ALHR can adapt well to the complex environment and confined spaces within the transformer ducts. It can nimbly bypass obstacles and smoothly navigate through curved and narrow pipelines to reach areas inaccessible to traditional inspection equipment, which verifies its application potential as a type of overheating monitoring robot.

Although this study validates the application potential of BP/WS2 moiré superlattices in constructing light-driven infrared-detecting anemone hydrogel robots, its significance extends beyond this specific material’s performance. It lies in presenting a universal design framework and integration strategy. This framework can be broadly applied to multifunctional soft robots based on diverse advanced two-dimensional materials, particularly moiré superlattice systems. As depicted in Fig. 5h, the designed soft robot features two core functional units: a driving module and a sensing module. On the one hand, the drive module must achieve controllable photothermal conversion with precise regulation of response intensity, speed, and spatial distribution. Integrated into a thermosensitive hydrogel matrix, this module induces material contraction/deformation through the photothermal effect. Material selection should prioritize moiré systems with high photothermal conversion efficiency (e.g., strongly coupled TMD heterojunctions and specific-angle graphene), or other 2D heterostructures suitable for flexible hydrogel environments (e.g., BP/Graphene, TMDs; see Supplementary Table 436,47–53). Preparation depends on achieving uniform nanomaterial dispersion within the hydrogel network, ensuring interface compatibility and long-term stability, achievable via optimized dispersion methods. On the other hand, the core requirements for the sensing module are efficient photoelectric detection within the target wavelength band, demanding high photoelectric conversion efficiency, a rapid response speed, excellent wavelength selectivity, and signal stability. Integrated onto a flexible structure, this module must achieve a drive-contact-conduction sequential response. Material selection prioritizes moiré systems with high photoelectric conversion efficiency and narrow or tunable response wavelengths (e.g., well-matched TMD heterojunctions, bandgap-tunable BP heterojunctions; see Supplementary Table 4). Fabrication primarily employs interfacial integration methods, with key challenges including strong adhesion between thin films and flexible substrates, efficient interfacial charge transport, and structural integrity.

Functional integration and response coordination between the drive and sensing modules are central to the system design. Drawing inspiration from nature’s intricate structure-function synergies, efficient biomimetic structural design effectively addresses this challenge. Furthermore, the tailored selection of sensing materials based on specific application requirements (e.g., environmental monitoring, drug delivery, environmental adaptation, and micro-sensing units) enables diverse signal detection and transmission capabilities.

In summary, this study achieves standardized integration of hydrogel robots through functional module decomposition and core requirement definition, guided by design principles of function-material matching, structure-function coupling, and response synergy. It provides a material-agnostic, universal methodology for systematically integrating the optoelectronic/photothermal properties of advanced two-dimensional materials with the flexibility, actuation, and biocompatibility of hydrogels. The successful application of BP/WS2 moiré superlattices in ALHR serves as a robust demonstration of this framework’s efficacy and versatility.

## Methods

Preparation Materials
Red phosphorus (RP, ≥ 99.99%), tungsten trioxide (WO3, ≥ 99.8%), ammonium fluoride (NH4F, ≥ 99.8%), N-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAM, ≥ 98%), diphenyl(2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl)phosphine oxide (TPO, 97%), and N,N’-Methylenebisacrylamide (BIS, 98%) were all purchased from Aladdin Chemical Co., Ltd. Precipitated sulfur (S, CP) and acetone (C3H6O, AR) were obtained from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA, average Mw 100,000-120,000) and hydrofluoric acid (48 wt.% in H2O, ≥ 99.99%) were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. Potassium hydroxide (KOH, AR) was procured from Guangdong Guanghua Sci-Tech Co., Ltd. Absolute ethanol (C2H5OH, AR) was bought from Tianjin Fuyu Fine Chemical Co., Ltd. All materials were used directly without purification, except for N-isopropylacrylamide.

Preparation of WS2
The Si/SiO2 substrate was immersed in acetone and cleaned in an ultrasonic cleaner for 15 min. Subsequently, it was rinsed with acetone, absolute ethanol, and deionized water for 5 min each to remove the organic matter and impurities remaining on the substrate surface. Then, it was fully dried in a vacuum drying oven. 600 mg of S powder was weighed and placed in a quartz boat as the sulfur source, and 40 mg of WO3 powder was taken and placed in another quartz boat as the tungsten source. The cleaned substrate was inverted above the WO3 powder. The two quartz boats were placed into a specially-made long quartz tube and then put into a dual-temperature-zone tube furnace. Argon was introduced as a protective gas. The temperature of the S powder was set at 200 °C, and that of WO3 was 850 °C. The system was heated for 30 min to ensure complete reaction. After the furnace temperature had completely dropped to room temperature, the substrate was taken out and rinsed three times with absolute ethanol and deionized water, respectively, to remove the surface residues. Thus, WS2 on the Si/SiO2 substrate was obtained.

Transfer of WS2 nanosheets
A sufficient amount of PMMA solution was spin-coated on the surface of WS2 on the Si/SiO2 substrate and heated at 80 °C for 2 min to ensure full adhesion between them. A supersaturated KOH solution was prepared, and the substrate with spin-coated PMMA was placed in the solution to separate WS2 from the substrate. The floating WS2/PMMA hybrid structure on the surface was rinsed multiple times with deionized water to remove the residual KOH solution. A BOE solution (20 g of ammonium fluoride, 30 mL of deionized water, and 7 mL of hydrofluoric acid) was prepared, and the Si/SiO2 substrate was soaked in it for 5 min to etch the window. The etched substrate was carefully used to pick up the WS2/PMMA hybrid structure and heated on a hot plate for 15 min to enhance its adhesion. The target substrate was immersed in acetone for 1 h to fully dissolve the PMMA. After being taken out, the surface was thoroughly cleaned with isopropanol and then dried with nitrogen. In this way, the WS2 nanosheet structure on the specific substrate was obtained.

Preparation of BP nanosheets
A certain amount of red phosphorus powder was mixed with grinding balls and placed in a planetary ball mill for 48 h of full mixing and ball-milling to obtain high-purity bulk black phosphorus powder. A certain amount of black phosphorus powder was fully stirred with absolute ethanol for 4 h to obtain a black phosphorus dispersion in absolute ethanol. The dispersion was placed in a double-layer beaker and subjected to ultrasonic treatment in a cold-water bath for 10 h to break the inter-layer van der Waals forces by the action of ultrasound. After centrifuging the dispersion at 2152 × g for 30 min, the supernatant was taken as the BP nanosheet dispersion.

Preparation of BP/WS2 composites
The BP nanosheet dispersion was uniformly sprayed on the surface of WS2 nanosheets using an inkjet printer and vacuum-dried in a vacuum drying oven for 4 h to improve the adhesion between them. After taking it out, Au electrodes were thermally evaporated inside and outside the window of the substrate, and thus the BP/WS2 composite on the Si/SiO2 substrate was obtained. The WS2 nanosheets on the substrate surface were scraped off, fully dispersed in absolute ethanol, and then ultrasonically blended with the BP nanosheet dispersion for 30 min to obtain the BP/WS2 composite dispersion. Through a series of preliminary experiments for optimization, the mass ratio of BP nanosheets to WS2 nanosheets was determined to be 1:8.

Preparation of Anemone-like Light-driven/light-detecting Hydrogel Robots
4.8 g of purified NIPAM powder, 0.12 g of TPO, and 0.13 g of BIS were taken and added with 2 mL of absolute ethanol and 7 mL of deionized water, and the mixture was stirred for 30 min to ensure full dissolution. The solution was placed in a vacuum oven and evacuated for 10 min to eliminate the internal bubbles. Then it was poured into a tentacle-shaped mold and refrigerated at 5 °C for 12 h to form a cross-linked colloid. For the base part of the anemone-like hydrogel robot, 2 mL of the BP/WS2 composite dispersion was used instead of absolute ethanol. Other operations were similar to those for the tentacle part. After defoaming, it was poured into the base mold and also refrigerated to form a colloid. After 12 h, it was taken out and cured under a 395-nm ultraviolet lamp for 10 min. Then the hydrogel was taken out and thoroughly rinsed with deionized water to remove the residual monomers on the surface. After assembling the tentacles and the base, it was soaked in deionized water for 3 h to fully swell. Finally, the BP/WS2 film was spin-coated on the tip of the tentacles and ALHR was obtained by low-temperature drying at 25 °C for 48 h. The substrate has a length of 20 mm, a width of 4 mm, and a thickness of approximately 3 mm. Each tentacle is 14 mm long and has a diameter of 2 mm. Six tentacles in total are arranged in a 3 × 2 configuration. The base plate contains 7.5-8% (by mass) of the BP/WS2 molar superlattice material and 50-65% (by mass) of water. The tentacles contain 2-3% (by mass) of the bimodal photoresponsive film and 50-65% (by mass) of water.

Equipment
Equipment: The surface morphology was characterized by a field emission scanning electron microscope (FEI, Verios G4) and a transmission electron microscope (FEI, Talos F200X). The phase composition of the material was analyzed using an X-ray diffractometer (D8 DISCOVER A25). For different types of spectroscopy and property analysis, the following equipment was used. Raman spectra were obtained with a micro-confocal Raman spectrometer (WItec, Alpha300R). An ultraviolet-visible spectrophotometer (Shimadzu, UV-3600) was employed for absorption spectroscopy, and a multi-functional parameter analyzer (Keithley, 4200A-SCS) was used for electrical property analysis. Specific wavelength illumination experiments were carried out using power-tunable 365 nm, 405 nm, 515 nm, 550 nm, 610 nm, 660 nm, 808 nm, and 940 nm lasers. The laser beams irradiated the sample perpendicularly. Under the monochromatic light of different wavelengths provided by a monochromator (Model Omni-λ3009, ZOLTAN HanGuang Co.), the optical response of the device was recorded by a source meter (Model 6517B, Keithley). The response times were measured with an oscilloscope equipped with an electronic shutter (Model MSO4054, Tektronix). Photothermal measurements were conducted using a light source with a fixed power density, which was calibrated to be 45.0 ± 0.5 mW/cm2 using an optical power meter (Model 1936-R, Newport). Unless otherwise stated, this power density was applied for all experiments. The surface temperature was measured by an infrared thermal imager (Hikvision, P10) at a data acquisition rate of 10 Hz.

Data availability
Relevant data supporting the key findings of this study are available within the article and the Supplementary Information file. All raw data generated during the current study are available from the corresponding authors upon request.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript presents the design of a multifunctional biomimetic hydrogel robot that integrates a BP/WS₂ moiré superlattice to achieve both photothermal actuation and photoelectric sensing for real-time overheating detection. This concept leverages the unique interlayer interactions between BP and WS₂ to enhance both photothermal and photovoltaic performance, and integrates this dual-function material into a PNIPAM hydrogel to create an anemone-inspired light-driven robot capable of directional locomotion and infrared radiation detection. The work is technically solid and represents a meaningful contribution to the integration of sensing and actuation in soft robotic systems. However, the scientific novelty lies more in the integration strategy and application demonstration than in a fundamental breakthrough in materials science or robotic mechanisms. Moiré superlattices themselves are not new, and their optoelectronic properties have been extensively reported. Thus, the conceptual advance of this work is largely application-driven rather than rooted in the discovery of new physics.
The abstract and introduction provide clear motivation for the need to integrate sensing and actuation functions in hydrogel robots and highlight the potential advantages of using moiré superlattices. However, the problem statement remains too general and does not sharply define the specific performance limitations of existing soft robots that the proposed system overcomes. To meet the high conceptual and scientific threshold of Nature Communications, the authors should more clearly articulate the scientific and technological gap and emphasize why BP/WS₂ moiré superlattice provides a distinct solution compared to existing photothermal or photoresponsive materials. This will strengthen the impact narrative of the manuscript.
The experimental work is thorough, including extensive material characterization (XRD, Raman, TEM, UPS, XPS, UV-Vis) that supports the formation of the moiré superlattice. The performance metrics reported such as the 72.1% photothermal conversion efficiency, 4.14 A/W responsivity, and 12 × 10¹¹ Jones detectivity, are impressive and support the claim of enhanced optoelectronic response. The robot demonstration is conceptually appealing, showing how the base and tentacle components can respond to light and infrared stimuli, respectively. However, the manuscript lacks quantitative benchmarking against state-of-the-art systems in terms of robot performance. Parameters such as actuation speed, bending displacement, response time, spatial resolution, and robustness under prolonged operation should be evaluated and compared to competing photothermal actuators. Moreover, the environmental stability and practical functionality of the robot should be further tested, especially under fluidic or more realistic pipeline conditions.
A significant weakness of the presentation is the absence of video demonstrations. Since the core of the work involves a soft robot that moves and senses based on photothermal and photoelectric cues, including high-quality supplementary videos would greatly strengthen the manuscript’s impact, making the concept more intuitive and convincing. Visual content would also help reviewers and readers better evaluate the claimed responsiveness and motion behavior, which is difficult to fully convey through static figures alone.
The discussion effectively explains the underlying mechanism of enhanced photothermal and photoelectric response through DFT calculations and analysis of energy band modulation. However, it is focused mainly on material properties and less on the broader design framework that this strategy enables for other multifunctional hydrogel robots. To elevate the conceptual weight of the work, the authors should extend the discussion to generalize this integration strategy beyond BP/WS₂ to other moiré or 2D systems, positioning it as a versatile platform for multifunctional soft robotics.
The manuscript is generally well written, but some sentences are overly long and descriptive, particularly in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The writing should be tightened for clarity, and the novelty should be emphasized more directly. In addition, the title should be revised to better reflect the main focus of the study. Currently, the title emphasizes the moiré superlattice but does not sufficiently highlight the hydrogel robot or its application in real-time thermal surveillance, which is the true strength of this work. A more application-reflective title may help align expectations and better communicate the contribution of the study.
Overall, this is a strong applied research paper with high-quality material characterization and a creative integration concept. However, in its current form, it may not fully meet the high conceptual threshold of Nature Communications. To improve its chances, the authors should: (i) sharpen the novelty and gap statement, (ii) provide quantitative robot performance benchmarking, (iii) add video demonstrations, (iv) revise the title for clarity and accuracy, and (v) generalize the discussion to strengthen conceptual significance. If these revisions are made, the work could be more competitive. At present, the most appropriate recommendation is major revision.

Our hydrogel robot is designed to fulfill two core functions: “mobility actuation” and

The radiation from overheated sources usually concentrates in the infrared spectrum. We chose
660 nm red light as the driving light source mainly to achieve significant spectral separation

2

illumination is significantly lower than that achievable with 808 nm radiation at the same light
intensity. This means the mechanical deformation signal from the driving light source itself is
strictly kept at a low level. This prevents contact with the active electrode, thus minimizing
interference with the overheating monitoring module and greatly improving the accuracy and
reliability of environmental hotspot detection.
The 808 nm light source in our study is not used as the driving light source but as a
demonstration light source. Its role is to simulate the infrared radiation from typical overheating
sources in the environment, so as to verify the robot's detection ability for such target signals.

scientific reasons:
1) Achieving functional decoupling by separating its spectrum from the target monitoring signal;
2) Enabling controllable and safe driving by utilizing the moderate photothermal response of
materials in this wavelength range; 3) Minimizing interference with the monitoring system due
to its weak response characteristics.

Response: We sincerely appreciate your thorough review of our work and the valuable
feedback you’ve provided. Your comments on the interpretation of the W 4f and P 2p peak
shifts in the XPS spectra are both relevant and significant. Below, we address each of your
concerns sequentially and elaborate on our supplementary analysis and discussion.
First, we’d like to clarify and emphasize the actual observations reported in our manuscript: W
4f peak: A decrease in binding energy (red shift) was observed. P 2p peak: An increase in
binding energy (blue shift) was observed. In the original manuscript, we incorrectly described
the decrease in W 4f binding energy as a blue shift. We sincerely apologize for this
typographical error. In the original manuscript, our explanation was that the moiré potential
modulated the electron density of W atoms. The formation of a flat band enhanced electron
localization, inducing a quantum confinement effect that facilitated electron movement within
confined orbitals. The P 2p blue shift is due to P atoms in BP acting as electron donors within
the heterojunction. To support our view, we tested the ultraviolet photoelectron spectra (UPS)
of intrinsic BP, WS , and BP/WS (Supplementary Fig. 5, Supplementary Fig. 6, and Fig. 2j).
2 2
Comparisons showed a significant downward shift in the Fermi level of the composite material
compared to pure WS . DFT calculations further indicated that the work function of the
2
composite material lies between those of BP and WS₂. For WS , the Fermi level shift shows
2
that the moiré potential effectively modulates the potential distribution of W atoms near the
interface, leading to the localization of their electron cloud. When electrons are localized around
W atoms, their shielding effect on W 4f inner-shell electrons is enhanced. According to
Coulomb’s law, this enhanced shielding weakens the nucleus’s effective attraction to 4f
electrons, thus reducing their binding energy. The composite material’s work function being
higher than that of BP means that, in the composite, BP acts as an electron donor. By transferring
electrons to WS , it reduces the surface electron density, enhancing the nucleus’s electron-
2
binding ability and increasing the work function compared to the intrinsic material.
We fully agree that surface charging effects must be excluded. During XPS testing, accumulated
positive charges on the sample surface can cause energy loss in all emitted photoelectrons,
resulting in an overall peak shift towards higher binding energies in the spectrum. We analyzed
the peak shifts of elements in the composite material: W 4f and S 2s were red-shifted, while P
2p was blue-shifted. This asynchronous shift pattern clearly rules out surface charging
interference, confirming that the peak shifts are due to changes in the chemical environment.
Additionally, during data processing, we used the C 1s peak (284.8 eV) from contaminant
carbon as an internal standard for calibration to reduce surface charging effects.
Black phosphorus is prone to oxidation. Despite our best efforts, partial surface oxidation was
inevitable during testing. However, as you can see, oxidation peaks for phosphorus are present
in both the pristine material and the composite. Importantly, the intensity of these oxidation
peaks is significantly lower in the composite (Fig. 2i). Comparing the two under the same
conditions allows us to effectively exclude interference from oxidation peaks of the composite
materials and focus on chemical state changes related to material composite formation.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript presents the design of a multifunctional biomimetic hydrogel robot that
integrates a BP/WS moiré superlattice to achieve both photothermal actuation and
2
photoelectric sensing for real-time overheating detection. This concept leverages the unique
interlayer interactions between BP and WS₂ to enhance both photothermal and photovoltaic
performance, and integrates this dual-function material into a PNIPAM hydrogel to create an
anemone-inspired light-driven robot capable of directional locomotion and infrared radiation
detection. The work is technically solid and represents a meaningful contribution to the
integration of sensing and actuation in soft robotic systems. However, the scientific novelty lies
more in the integration strategy and application demonstration than in a fundamental
breakthrough in materials science or robotic mechanisms. Moiré superlattices themselves are
not new, and their optoelectronic properties have been extensively reported. Thus, the
conceptual advance of this work is largely application-driven rather than rooted in the discovery
of new physics.
The abstract and introduction provide clear motivation for the need to integrate sensing and
actuation functions in hydrogel robots and highlight the potential advantages of using moiré
superlattices. However, the problem statement remains too general and does not sharply define
the specific performance limitations of existing soft robots that the proposed system overcomes.
To meet the high conceptual and scientific threshold of Nature Communications, the authors
should more clearly articulate the scientific and technological gap and emphasize why BP/WS
2
moiré superlattice provides a distinct solution compared to existing photothermal or
photoresponsive materials. This will strengthen the impact narrative of the manuscript.
The experimental work is thorough, including extensive material characterization (XRD,
Raman, TEM, UPS, XPS, UV-Vis) that supports the formation of the moiré superlattice. The
performance metrics reported such as the 72.1% photothermal conversion efficiency, 4.14 A/W
responsivity, and 12 × 1011 Jones detectivity, are impressive and support the claim of enhanced
optoelectronic response. The robot demonstration is conceptually appealing, showing how the
base and tentacle components can respond to light and infrared stimuli, respectively. However,
the manuscript lacks quantitative benchmarking against state-of-the-art systems in terms of
robot performance. Parameters such as actuation speed, bending displacement, response time,
spatial resolution, and robustness under prolonged operation should be evaluated and
compared to competing photothermal actuators. Moreover, the environmental stability and practical
functionality of the robot should be further tested, especially under fluidic or more realistic
pipeline conditions.
A significant weakness of the presentation is the absence of video demonstrations. Since the
core of the work involves a soft robot that moves and senses based on photothermal and
photoelectric cues, including high-quality supplementary videos would greatly strengthen the
manuscript’s impact, making the concept more intuitive and convincing. Visual content would
also help reviewers and readers better evaluate the claimed responsiveness and motion behavior,
which is difficult to fully convey through static figures alone.
The discussion effectively explains the underlying mechanism of enhanced photothermal and
photoelectric response through DFT calculations and analysis of energy band modulation.
However, it is focused mainly on material properties and less on the broader design framework
that this strategy enables for other multifunctional hydrogel robots. To elevate the conceptual
weight of the work, the authors should extend the discussion to generalize this integration
strategy beyond BP/WS to other moiré or 2D systems, positioning it as a versatile platform for
2
multifunctional soft robotics.
The manuscript is generally well written, but some sentences are overly long and descriptive,
particularly in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The writing should be tightened for
clarity, and the novelty should be emphasized more directly. In addition, the title should be
revised to better reflect the main focus of the study. Currently, the title emphasizes the
moiré superlattice but does not sufficiently highlight the hydrogel robot or its application in
real-time thermal surveillance, which is the true strength of this work. A more application-reflective
title may help align expectations and better communicate the contribution of the study.
Overall, this is a strong applied research paper with high-quality material characterization and
a creative integration concept. However, in its current form, it may not fully meet the high
conceptual threshold of Nature Communications. To improve its chances, the authors should:
(i) sharpen the novelty and gap statement, (ii) provide quantitative robot performance
benchmarking, (iii) add video demonstrations, (iv) revise the title for clarity and accuracy, and
(v) generalize the discussion to strengthen conceptual significance. If these revisions are made,
the work could be more competitive. At present, the most appropriate recommendation is major
revision.

the revised version has significantly improved in terms of academic rigor, clarity, and

combination of high-performance moiré superlattice materials and hydrogels; (2) A

Second, we completely rewrote the introduction. We weakened the background

Finally, we also made a corresponding response in the conclusion section. Instead of

of this work in the design paradigm and material application, emphasizing its leading
role in future research. The specific revised content is quoted as follows:
“Abstract
The flexibility and intelligent responsiveness of hydrogel robots offer great potential for
exploration in narrow and complex environments. However, it remains challenging to
stably and efficiently integrate sensors with hydrogel robotic bodies. Inspired by marine
organisms, this paper presents an anemone-like light-driven hydrogel robot (ALHR) for
directional infrared radiation detection. Using the regulation of photo-generated
carriers by moiré superlattices and the synergistic photo-thermal-electric effects, a
black phosphorus/tungsten disulfide (BP/WS ) moiré superlattice was fabricated
2
through ultrasonic-assisted stacking, which shows excellent dual-mode photothermal-
photovoltaic conversion performance. Based on this, a composite poly(N-
isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) hydrogel was used to build the base plate and tentacle
structures of the ALHR. Specific illumination triggers the photothermal effect of the
BP/WS moiré superlattice, allowing for directional movement. When the tentacles
2
retract and contact the bottom electrode, photocurrent signals are conducted for
infrared detection. The ALHR can work in specialized spatial environments, providing
a new method for early overheating fault identification. This study also proposes a
design framework for multifunctional hydrogel robots. By integrating responsive units
with flexible substrates to achieve coupled synergistic responses, its material properties
enable various functionalities, offering a universal platform and model for developing
multifunctional soft robots based on advanced low dimensional materials.
Main
Flexible hydrogel robots with biomimetic structures show great application potential in
complex scenarios that humans can't access, like deep-sea exploration, extremely
confined spaces, and high-radiation environments. This is due to their excellent
biocompatibility, deformability, and environmental adaptability [1-4]. By integrating
functional units such as sensors and actuators into hydrogel matrices to imitate the
morphology and behavior of natural organisms, researchers can effectively combine
the unique physicochemical properties of hydrogels with the excellent capabilities of
biological systems [5-8]. This method gives robots intelligent features like autonomous
mobility and real-time perception, creating new opportunities for the development of
flexible bionic robots [9-11]. However, two main bottlenecks still exist in this field. Firstly,
the high water content and softness of hydrogels often reduce the performance and
stability of integrated sensors, making traditional microelectronic fabrication
techniques inappropriate. Secondly, current research mainly focuses on achieving
single functions (such as actuation or drug delivery) and has difficulty in balancing
robotic mobility and sensing capabilities. Achieving the integration of actuation-
sensing remains a very challenging task [12, 13]. Therefore, how to enhance the response
speed, structural stability, and sensing compatibility of hydrogel robots simultaneously
through innovative material and structural design has become a crucial scientific
problem that needs urgent solutions in this field.
To tackle these challenges, exploring novel materials that combine both actuation and
sensing functions is a key breakthrough. Among different actuation strategies, light-
driven actuation is regarded as an ideal option for building smart hydrogel robots. This
is because it is non-contact, highly precise, has a rapid response, and excellent
biocompatibility [14-20]. Among them, poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM), due to
its excellent thermosensitive properties, has become a typical material system for
preparing photodriven hydrogels when combined with photothermal converters [21-23].
Traditional methods rely on complex integrated designs to couple sensing and driving
functions, but this makes the system even more unstable [24, 25]. Therefore, developing
an intrinsic, integrated material with both photothermal actuation and optoelectronic
sensing capabilities is the fundamental solution to the sensor-hydrogel compatibility
problem. Our research focuses on emerging moiré superlattice materials. This periodic
structure, formed by stacking two two-dimensional(2D) materials with different lattice
constants or orientations [26, 27], provides a unique moiré potential field. This field can
effectively adjust interlayer exciton dynamics, phonon vibration modes, and band
structures, offering an unprecedented platform for synergistically optimizing
photothermal and photovoltaic performance [28-37]. Despite the great potential of moiré
superlattices, current research mainly focuses on systems such as graphene. There is
still limited systematic exploration of heterojunctions and their dual-function
characteristics involving BP, a material with an inherently high photothermal
coefficient, and other 2D materials.
This work introduces a research paradigm advancing from novel materials to novel
designs and culminating in a universal framework to realize multifunctional integrated
hydrogel robots. At the materials level, we designed and synthesized black
phosphorus/tungsten disulfide (BP/WS ) moiré superlattices using an ultrasonic-
2
assisted stacking method. The moiré potential field in this material enhances phonon-
photon coupling to improve photothermal conversion efficiency while simultaneously
promoting the separation and transport of photogenerated carriers, resulting in
exceptional dual photothermal-photovoltaic response characteristics. At the design
level, inspired by sea anemone feeding behavior, we integrated the BP/WS moiré
2
superlattice with a PNIPAM flexible matrix to construct an anemone-like light-driven
hydrogel robot (ALHR). The base plate generates photothermal effects under
illumination to drive directional motion, while the tentacles sense infrared radiation
and produce photocurrent signals, effectively integrating coordinated motion and
sensing. Finally, we propose a universal strategy centered on function-oriented moiré
superlattice-hydrogels, where modular integration and synergistic coupling of
responsive units with flexible substrates enable on-demand design of intelligent soft
robots with diverse sensing and actuation capabilities. This research not only provides
new materials and methods for high-performance integrated actuator-sensor robots but
also establishes a universal technical pathway and design paradigm for future
multifunctional soft robots based on advanced 2D materials.
Conclusion
Inspired by the biological activity patterns of sea anemones, this study developed an
anemone-like light-driven hydrogel robot that can detect superheating, and thus
proposed a universal fabrication strategy for multifunctional hydrogel robots.
Specifically, BP/WS moiré superlattice materials were first synthesized by ultrasonic -
2
assisted stacking. These materials have long-range periodic moiré patterns. Their
modulation effect causes interfacial electron rearrangement, enhances partial electron
localization, and significantly affects the system's light absorption properties.
Experiments confirmed that BP/WS moiré superlattices have improved photothermal
2
and photovoltaic conversion capabilities in the infrared spectrum. Based on this, we
fully used the excellent photothermal response and specific photoconductive properties
of the BP/WS moiré superlattice material. By integrating it as a dual-functional
2
material for both actuation and sensing into PNIPAM hydrogel, we designed and made
the ALHR. Under specific illumination, this robot can move flexibly driven by light
through its photothermal response and can recognize infrared radiation.
We further propose a fabrication framework for moiré superlattice material-hydrogel
based soft robots. Focusing on function-oriented material selection and inspired by
biomimetic structures, this approach allows the preparation of hydrogel robots with
replaceable modules, expandable functions, and controllable synergistic behavior. This
provides a general technical way and design model for the future design and fabrication
of multifunctional soft robots based on advanced two-dimensional materials.”

Fig. 5| h Implementation paradigm of multifunctional hydrogel robots based on moiré
superlattice materials.
Although this study validates the application potential of BP/WS moiré superlattices
2
in constructing light-driven infrared-detecting anemone hydrogel robots, its core
significance extends beyond this specific material’s performance. It lies in presenting
a universal design framework and integration strategy. This framework can be broadly
applied to multifunctional soft robots based on diverse advanced two-dimensional
materials, particularly moiré superlattice systems. As depicted in Fig. 5h, the designed
soft robot features two core functional units: a driving module and a sensing module.
The drive module must achieve controllable photothermal conversion with precise
regulation of response intensity, speed, and spatial distribution. Integrated into a
thermosensitive hydrogel matrix, this module induces material contraction/deformation
through the photothermal effect. Material selection should prioritize moiré systems with
high photothermal conversion efficiency (e.g., strongly coupled TMD heterojunctions
and specific-angle graphene), or other 2D heterostructures suitable for flexible
hydrogel environments (e.g., BP/Graphene, TMDs; see Supplementary Information
Table 4). Preparation depends on achieving uniform nanomaterial dispersion within
the hydrogel network, ensuring interface compatibility and long-term stability,
achievable via optimized dispersion methods.
The core requirements for the sensing module are efficient photoelectric detection
within the target wavelength band, demanding high photoelectric conversion efficiency,
a rapid response speed, excellent wavelength selectivity, and signal stability. Integrated
onto a flexible structure, this module must achieve a drive-contact-conduction
sequential response. Material selection prioritizes moiré systems with high
photoelectric conversion efficiency and narrow or tunable response wavelengths (e.g.,
well-matched TMD heterojunctions, bandgap-tunable BP heterojunctions; see
Supplementary Information, Table 4). Fabrication primarily employs interfacial
integration methods, with key challenges including strong adhesion between thin films
and flexible substrates, efficient interfacial charge transport, and structural integrity.
Functional integration and response coordination between the drive and sensing
modules are central to the system design. Drawing inspiration from nature's intricate
structure-function synergies, efficient biomimetic structural design effectively
addresses this challenge. Furthermore, the tailored selection of sensing materials based
on specific application requirements (e.g., environmental monitoring, drug delivery,
environmental adaptation, and micro-sensing units) enables diverse signal detection
and transmission capabilities.
In summary, this study achieves standardized integration of hydrogel robots through
functional module decomposition and core requirement definition, guided by design
principles of function-material matching, structure-function coupling, and response
synergy. It provides a material-agnostic, universal methodology for systematically
integrating the optoelectronic/photothermal properties of advanced two-dimensional
materials with the flexibility, actuation, and biocompatibility of hydrogels. The
successful application of BP/WS moiré superlattices in ALHR serves as a robust
2
demonstration of this framework’s efficacy and versatility. Moving forward, as more
high-performance two-dimensional moiré systems are discovered, manufacturing
techniques advance, and hydrogel functionalization research deepens, this framework
will serve as a valuable catalyst for developing next-generation intelligent soft robots
with integrated sensing-actuation capabilities. This will advance innovations in critical
fields including environmental monitoring, healthcare, and industrial applications.

### Reviewer 2

The revised manuscript has greatly improved and the previous concerns have been addressed. Thus the revised manuscript can be accepted for publication.

### Reviewer 3

I appreciate the authors’ careful and thorough revision of the manuscript in response to my comments. The revised version demonstrates substantial improvement in conceptual framing, experimental rigor, and presentation quality.
In particular, the revised title more accurately reflects the core contribution of the work by emphasizing the hydrogel robot and its multifunctional integration, rather than focusing narrowly on the moiré superlattice material alone. The Abstract and Introduction have been significantly strengthened, with a clearer articulation of the scientific and technological gap, and a more convincing positioning of the work as an integration-driven design framework for multifunctional hydrogel robots rather than a purely materials-centric advance. The addition of quantitative benchmarking data for robot performance including actuation speed, stability, repeatability, spatial resolution, and environmental adaptability, greatly enhances the credibility of the claims and allows meaningful comparison with existing photothermal soft robotic systems. While the advance remains application- and integration-driven rather than a fundamental discovery in moiré physics, the revised manuscript now presents a coherent, well-supported, and impactful contribution.
